lead: Grammar classes are graded by how tightly the two sides of each rule are tied. Type 0 has almost no restriction, type 1 keeps length from shrinking, type 2 has one variable on the left, and type 3 has a single terminal plus at most one variable. This ladder matches four machines and four language classes. Compiler writers use type 2 and type 3 daily; researchers use type 0 and type 1 to mark the edge of decidability.
prereq: You need: 3.1 to 3.6, and Unit 2 for regular languages.

blocks.text: A grammar has variables (also called nonterminals), terminals and a start symbol. The Chomsky type fixes the shape of every production. Write α, β, γ for strings of variables and terminals, and A, B for single variables.

items: Type 0 (unrestricted): α → β, where α contains at least one variable. β may be any string, including ε.
Type 1 (context-sensitive): αAβ → αγβ with γ ≠ ε. Equivalent form: every rule is non-contracting, |left| ≤ |right|. One exception: S → ε is allowed if S never appears on a right side.
Type 2 (context-free): A → α. The left side is exactly one variable.
Type 3 (regular): right-linear A → aB or A → a, or left-linear A → Ba or A → a. A grammar may use one direction; both directions give the same language class.

blocks.text: Some syllabi call type 0 phrase-structure grammars. The numbering runs from the most powerful type to the weakest: 0 is strongest, 3 is weakest. Every type 3 grammar is also type 2, every type 2 is type 1, and every type 1 is type 0.
Each grammar type has a matching machine and a matching language class.
The inclusions are strict. A witness separates each neighbouring pair.

items: 3.6 shows aⁿbⁿcⁿ is not context-free; a context-sensitive grammar generates it. So context-free ⊂ context-sensitive.
Unit 2 pumping lemma shows aⁿbⁿ is not regular; the grammar S → aSb | ε makes it context-free. So regular ⊂ context-free.

The halting set is recursively enumerable but not recursive (Unit 6). Every context-sensitive language is recursive, so the halting set is type 0 and not type 1. So context-sensitive ⊂ recursively enumerable.

blocks.text: A linear bounded automaton is a Turing machine whose tape is limited to the input length. That limit is exactly what non-contracting rules enforce: no derivation step can shrink the sentential form, so the machine never needs more cells than the input.

To classify a language, test from the weakest type upward. Try a regular expression or a finite automaton first. If that fails, give a context-free grammar. If that fails, give a context-sensitive grammar. If the language is not recursive, only type 0 is possible.

items: Look for a pattern that needs unbounded counting with one counter: aⁿbⁿ. That is context-free, not regular.
Two counters that must stay equal, as in aⁿbⁿcⁿ, need context-sensitive rules; the pumping lemma for context-free languages proves it is not type 2.
A set defined by halting or by an undecidable property is type 0; Unit 6 supplies the proof that it is not recursive.

blocks.text: Do not confuse left-linear with right-linear. A grammar that mixes both directions, such as A → aB and B → Ab in one chain, may generate a non-regular language. Type 3 requires one consistent direction, or the equivalent finite automaton.

figure.caption: Each ring is one grammar type, with the machine that accepts it; outer rings allow more. The worked example’s four languages are the witnesses: aᵐbⁿ is regular, aⁿbⁿ is context-free but not regular, aⁿbⁿcⁿ is context-sensitive but not context-free, and the halting set is type 0 only.

spec.aria: Four nested rings: type 3 regular with aᵐbⁿ, type 2 context-free with aⁿbⁿ, type 1 context-sensitive with aⁿbⁿcⁿ, type 0 unrestricted with the halting set, each labelled with its rule shape and machine.

examples.question: Classify each language by the smallest grammar type that generates it. (1) L1 = {aᵐbⁿ | m, n ≥ 0}. (2) L2 = {aⁿbⁿ | n ≥ 0}. (3) L3 = {aⁿbⁿcⁿ | n ≥ 0}. (4) L4 = {⟨M, w⟩ : M halts on w}.
steps: L1 has all a's before all b's, with any counts. Grammar: S → aS | B, B → bB | ε. This is right-linear, so L1 is regular, type 3.
L2 pairs each a with one b. Grammar: S → aSb | ε. This is context-free, type 2. The pumping lemma for regular languages in Unit 2 proves no type 3 grammar exists.

L3 has three equal counts. A context-sensitive grammar for n ≥ 1 is: S′ → S | ε; S → aSBC | aBC; CB → BC; aB → ab; bB → bb; bC → bc; cC → cc. The rule CB → BC is not context-free because its left side has two variables. The pumping lemma in 3.6 proves no type 2 grammar exists. So L3 is type 1.
L4 is the halting set. Unit 6 proves it is recursively enumerable but not recursive. Every context-sensitive language is recursive, so L4 cannot be type 1, type 2 or type 3. It is type 0 only.
examples.answer: L1 is type 3, L2 is type 2, L3 is type 1, and L4 is type 0.

traps: The numbers run from most powerful to weakest: type 0 is strongest, type 3 is weakest. Do not call type 3 the strongest grammar.
Saying aⁿbⁿcⁿ is context-sensitive is only half the answer. The exam also wants the proof that it is not context-free, usually by the pumping lemma in 3.6.
Type 1 allows S → ε only when the start symbol S never appears on a right side. Otherwise every type 1 rule must be non-contracting.
A type 0 left side must contain at least one variable. A rule such as a → b, with only terminals on the left, is not a valid type 0 production.
A grammar that mixes left-linear and right-linear rules in one chain is not automatically type 3. Type 3 needs one consistent direction.

quiz.q: List the four Chomsky types in order from most powerful to weakest, and give the machine for each.
quiz.a: Type 0: Turing machine. Type 1: linear bounded automaton. Type 2: pushdown automaton. Type 3: finite automaton.

quiz.q: Why is every type 2 grammar also a type 1 grammar, apart from the special ε rule?
quiz.a: A type 2 rule A → α has one variable on the left. If α is not ε, both sides have length at least 1 and the rule is non-contracting. The only ε rule needed is S → ε, and type 1 allows it when S is not on a right side.

quiz.q: Write a type 3 grammar for the language a*b* and state whether it is right-linear or left-linear.
quiz.a: S → aS | B, B → bB | ε. The rules S → aS and B → bB have the form A → aB, and B → ε ends the string. The grammar is right-linear.

quiz.q: Give a context-sensitive rule that is not context-free, and explain why it is type 1.
quiz.a: Example: CB → BC. The left side contains the variable B and has length 2; the right side has length 2, so the rule is non-contracting. It is not type 2 because the left side has two symbols, not one variable.

quiz.q: The language {aⁿbⁿ} is context-free but not regular. Which two witnesses in the hierarchy does this single language separate?
quiz.a: It belongs to type 2 and not to type 3. So it separates context-free from regular: regular ⊂ context-free. The grammar S → aSb | ε generates it, and the regular pumping lemma proves no finite automaton accepts it.

quiz.q: The halting set is recursively enumerable. Which Chomsky type generates it, and why can it not be type 1?
quiz.a: It is type 0. Context-sensitive languages are accepted by linear bounded automata, which always halt, so every type 1 language is recursive. The halting set is not recursive (Unit 6), so it cannot be type 1.

quiz.q: What is another name for a type 0 grammar, and why does the numbering start at 0?
quiz.a: Another name is phrase-structure grammar. The numbering starts at 0 because type 0 is the most powerful class; later numbers add restrictions and give weaker classes.

beyond: Not for the exam. The Chomsky hierarchy was introduced by Noam Chomsky in the 1950s and is still used in linguistics and in compiler construction. Parser generators work mostly with type 2 grammars, while lexers use type 3. Newer grammar formalisms such as mildly context-sensitive grammars sit between type 1 and type 2 for natural language. Search next for "Chomsky hierarchy", "linear bounded automaton" and "mildly context-sensitive grammar".
